items.title: [Sports Science 101 #13] The Cheapest Medicine Most of Us Aren't Taking
items.body:
> Regular physical activity is one of the most effective, lowest-cost tools we have for preventing chronic diseases like type 2 diabetes, heart disease, and high blood pressure — and the required "dose" is smaller than most people think.

## Today's Concept

Chronic diseases — heart disease, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and several cancers — develop slowly over years and are the leading causes of death in the United States. Unlike infections, you can't catch them from someone else. They grow out of long-term patterns: what we eat, how we sleep, whether we smoke, and — the focus of today's lecture — how much we move.

Here's the core idea sports scientists want you to remember: **exercise works like a medicine, with a dose and a response.** When you do moderate aerobic activity (brisk walking counts), your muscles pull sugar out of the bloodstream more efficiently, a property called *insulin sensitivity*. Your heart pumps more blood per beat, your blood vessels stay more flexible, and resting blood pressure tends to drift down. Strength training adds muscle mass, which acts like a bigger "storage tank" for blood sugar and keeps your metabolism working in older age.

The official U.S. Physical Activity Guidelines translate this science into a prescription: **at least 150 minutes of moderate activity per week, plus muscle-strengthening activity on 2 or more days.** That's about 30 minutes of brisk walking, five days a week. And the dose-response curve has an encouraging shape: the biggest health gains come from going from *nothing* to *something*. Even 10-minute bouts count.

One more finding worth knowing: sitting for most of the day is a risk factor on its own, called *sedentary behavior*. A single workout doesn't fully cancel out 10 uninterrupted hours in a chair, so researchers recommend breaking up long sitting periods with short movement breaks.

How strong is the evidence? In the landmark U.S. Diabetes Prevention Program, adults with prediabetes who adopted a lifestyle program built around 150 minutes of weekly activity (plus modest weight loss) reduced their risk of developing type 2 diabetes by **58%** — a bigger reduction than the group taking the drug metformin achieved.

## In Everyday Life

Meet Dana, a 45-year-old accountant in Columbus, Ohio. Their annual checkup comes back with an A1C in the prediabetes range and borderline-high blood pressure. The doctor doesn't reach for the prescription pad first — they hand Dana an "exercise prescription."

Dana's plan costs almost nothing. Monday through Friday, they park at the far end of the office lot and take a brisk 15-minute walk at lunch around the block, then another 15 minutes with the dog after dinner. That's 150 minutes a week without a gym. On Saturdays, they do a 20-minute bodyweight routine from a free video — squats, push-ups, rows with a $25 pair of dumbbells from a sporting goods store.

Compare the price tags. The CDC estimates that a person diagnosed with diabetes faces thousands of dollars a year in extra medical costs — often more than $10,000 annually between medications, supplies, and doctor visits, even with insurance. Dana's "treatment"? A pair of walking shoes and a set of dumbbells, under $150 total. Six months later, their A1C is back in the normal range. Not every case turns around this cleanly — genetics and other factors matter — but the direction of the effect is one of the most consistent findings in health science.

## 3-Line Recap

1. Chronic diseases develop over years, and regular physical activity is a proven, low-cost way to lower the risk of many of them.
2. The target dose is 150 minutes of moderate activity per week plus 2 days of strength work — and going from zero to *anything* produces the steepest benefit.
3. Long uninterrupted sitting is its own risk factor, so breaking up sedentary time matters in addition to workouts.

## ✅ Self-Quiz

**Q1.** According to U.S. guidelines, the minimum recommended amount of moderate aerobic activity per week is:
- (a) 60 minutes
- (b) 150 minutes
- (c) 300 minutes

**Q2.** True or False: If you complete a hard 1-hour workout in the morning, sitting for the rest of the day carries no health risk.

**Q3.** In the Diabetes Prevention Program study, the lifestyle-change group (exercise plus modest weight loss) reduced their risk of developing type 2 diabetes by about:
- (a) 15%
- (b) 33%
- (c) 58%

## 📚 Today's Terms

- **Chronic disease**: A long-lasting condition, such as heart disease or type 2 diabetes, that develops gradually and usually can't be cured by a single treatment — but can often be prevented or managed.
- **Insulin sensitivity**: How effectively your body's cells respond to insulin and absorb sugar from the blood; exercise improves it.
- **Dose-response relationship**: The pattern where more of a treatment (here, physical activity) produces more of an effect — with the largest gains occurring when starting from zero.
- **Sedentary behavior**: Waking time spent sitting or reclining with very low energy use; a health risk factor independent of exercise habits.
- **Moderate-intensity activity**: Movement that raises your heart rate and breathing but still lets you hold a conversation — brisk walking is the classic example.

---

*Answers: Q1 — (b). The guideline is at least 150 minutes of moderate activity per week, plus strength training on 2 or more days. Q2 — False. Prolonged uninterrupted sitting is an independent risk factor, so one workout doesn't fully offset an otherwise sedentary day; short movement breaks help. Q3 — (c). The lifestyle group cut their diabetes risk by 58%, outperforming the medication (metformin) group in that study.*

items.title: [AFA 2025] Companies Look Greener Than Ever. The Pollution Didn't Go Anywhere.
items.body:
> An award-winning study finds that many firms "clean up" not by cutting emissions, but by selling their dirtiest plants to less-scrutinized buyers — pollution stays the same, while the seller's ESG image improves.

## What Was Presented

At the American Finance Association's 2025 Annual Meeting, the Dimensional Fund Advisors Prize (Distinguished Paper) went to "Sustainability or Greenwashing: Evidence from the Asset Market for Industrial Pollution" by Ran Duchin (Boston College), Janet Gao (Georgetown University), and Qiping Xu (University of Illinois Gies College of Business). The paper was published in the Journal of Finance.

The researchers asked a simple but uncomfortable question: when a company under environmental pressure announces it has become more sustainable, did it actually reduce pollution — or did it just sell the polluting part of itself to someone else?

To find out, they merged two datasets: the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency's Toxics Release Inventory, which tracks emissions at individual industrial plants over time, and corporate deal records from the Securities Data Company. This let them follow roughly 888 divestitures of industrial plants — refineries, chemical plants, steel operations — between 2000 and 2020, watching what happened to each plant's emissions after it changed hands.

The pattern they found is striking:

- Firms facing strong environmental pressure (from investors, regulators, or the public) are more likely to sell off their most pollutive plants.
- The buyers tend to be firms facing much weaker environmental pressure — often private companies with less public scrutiny — and frequently ones that already have supply-chain relationships or joint ventures with the seller.
- After the sale, the plants' pollution does not decline. The smokestacks keep running; only the name on the ownership papers changes.
- Meanwhile, the sellers talk up their sustainability record on earnings calls, earn higher stock returns as they shed pollutive plants, receive better ESG ratings, and enjoy lower environmental compliance costs.

The authors call this a "cosmetic" redrawing of the firm's boundary. Because sellers often keep buying from the very plants they sold, the underlying production — and the pollution — continues largely as before. As Xu put it, the result is a market splitting into two segments: "a green sector that appears greener, and a sector that keeps getting dirtier."

## Why It Matters

ESG investing directs trillions of dollars based on the idea that rewarding "green" companies and punishing "brown" ones will push the real economy toward lower emissions. This paper documents a major leak in that pipeline.

For investors, it means an improving ESG score is not automatic proof of environmental progress. A company can raise its rating by transferring assets rather than transforming them — and the study finds that rating agencies, regulators, and prosocial investors largely fail to catch the difference.

For business leaders and professionals working in sustainability, the finding is a career-relevant warning. Divestiture-driven "decarbonization" can look great in a sustainability report, but if the assets simply move to a less transparent owner, the company has managed appearances, not risk. As disclosure rules tighten and scrutiny of supply chains grows, strategies built on paper transfers become increasingly fragile.

For policymakers, the study suggests that measuring pollution by who legally owns a plant creates an easy loophole. If accountability follows ownership only, pollution will migrate to wherever oversight is weakest — a shell game with real environmental stakes.

## An Easy Analogy

Imagine a household that wants to brag about going car-free. Instead of giving up driving, they "sell" their gas-guzzling car to a cousin next door — then keep riding in that same car whenever they need it. On paper, the household owns zero cars and looks admirably green. In reality, the same engine burns the same fuel on the same streets. That is essentially what the paper documents at industrial scale: the pollution doesn't stop; it just changes whose name is on the title.

## 3-Line Summary

1. Firms under environmental pressure sell their dirtiest plants — often to less-scrutinized, related buyers — instead of cleaning them up.
2. Plant-level EPA data shows pollution does not fall after these sales, yet sellers gain better ESG ratings, higher returns, and lower compliance costs.
3. The paper, honored with the Dimensional Fund Advisors Distinguished Paper Prize, shows that tracking legal ownership instead of actual emissions leaves ESG systems open to greenwashing.

## 📚 Today's Terms

- **Greenwashing**: Making a company appear more environmentally friendly than it actually is, through marketing or accounting maneuvers rather than real change.
- **Divestiture**: The sale of a business unit or asset — here, an industrial plant — to another owner.
- **ESG rating**: A score assessing a company's environmental, social, and governance performance, widely used by investors to guide capital.
- **Toxics Release Inventory (TRI)**: A U.S. EPA program that publicly tracks toxic chemical releases from individual industrial facilities.
- **Firm boundary**: The line defining what a company legally owns and operates; the paper shows firms can redraw it "cosmetically" to shift pollution off their books.

items.title: The Wage-Inflation Trap: Why a 3.5% Raise Can Still Feel Like a Pay Cut in 2026
items.body:
Getting a raise is supposed to feel like progress. You sit down with your manager, you hear a number — 3%, 3.5%, maybe 4% if the year went well — and you walk out with the sense that next year will be a little easier than this one.

Then the grocery bill arrives. The insurance renewal lands. The rent letter shows up. And by spring, the raise has quietly disappeared into the ordinary business of living.

This is the wage-inflation trap: the gap between the raise on your pay stub and the raise your household budget actually experiences. It is not a conspiracy, and it is not a sign that you are managing money badly. It is arithmetic — and understanding the arithmetic is the first step to negotiating, budgeting, and planning around it.

---

## Nominal vs. real: the only two numbers that matter

Economists split pay into two ideas:

- **Nominal wages** — the dollar figure in your offer letter or pay stub.
- **Real wages** — that figure adjusted for what prices have done since.

Nominal pay is what you're told. Real pay is what you can buy.

The conversion is simple. Instead of subtracting inflation from your raise, divide:

```
Real change ≈ (1 + raise) ÷ (1 + inflation) − 1
```

Say you receive a 3.5% raise while the prices you personally face rise 4.2%:

```
(1.035 ÷ 1.042) − 1 = −0.0067  →  about −0.7%
```

You earned more dollars and bought less with them. Subtracting gives roughly the same answer at small numbers (3.5 − 4.2 = −0.7), so the shortcut is fine for a quick check — but the division method is the one that stays accurate when inflation runs high.

Flip the inputs and the story flips too. A 3.5% raise against 2.8% inflation is a genuine gain of about 0.7%. The raise itself is neutral. Everything depends on what it is measured against.

---

## Why headline inflation and your inflation aren't the same number

Here is the part that trips up most people: the inflation rate reported in the news is an average across a representative basket of goods and services. Almost nobody buys the average basket.

Official inflation gauges weight categories by how much a typical household spends on each. But your household has its own weights — and if your money is concentrated in the categories rising fastest, your **personal inflation rate** runs above the headline figure even when the headline figure is behaving.

A simplified illustration of how two households can experience the same economy differently:

| Household profile | Spending concentrated in | Effect on personal inflation |
|---|---|---|
| Renter, long commute, young kids | Rent, fuel, childcare, groceries | Typically **above** headline |
| Homeowner with a fixed low-rate mortgage, remote work | Housing cost locked in, minimal fuel | Typically **at or below** headline |
| Household with high medical utilization | Premiums, out-of-pocket care | Sensitive to health-cost trends |

*(Illustrative profiles, not measured data — the point is the mechanism, not the magnitudes.)*

Services, housing, insurance, and care-related costs have generally been the stickier part of the inflation picture in recent years, while goods prices have swung around more. Households whose budgets tilt toward the sticky categories feel the squeeze first and longest — which is why "inflation is coming down" and "my budget is tighter than last year" can both be true at the same time.

**Rule of thumb:** the lower your income, the larger the share of it goes to necessities, and the less room you have to substitute your way out of a price increase. That is why the same national inflation number lands unevenly across the workforce.

---

## The quiet deductions that shrink the raise before you see it

Even before inflation touches your paycheck, the headline raise gets trimmed:

1. **Benefit cost-sharing.** If your share of the health premium rises faster than your salary, part of the raise is absorbed on the way out the door. A raise that looks like 3.5% gross can land closer to 3% in take-home terms.
2. **Bracket and threshold effects.** Federal brackets and the standard deduction are indexed to inflation, which limits classic "bracket creep." But not every threshold in the tax and benefits system is indexed the same way — some phase-outs, credits, state-level parameters, and eligibility cutoffs move slowly or not at all. Crossing one can claw back more than the raise delivered.
3. **Contribution ratchets.** Retirement contributions set as a percentage of pay rise automatically with the raise. That is good long-term behavior — but it means the raise shows up in your 401(k) balance, not your checking account.
4. **The timing gap.** Prices move continuously. Raises arrive once a year. Even a raise that fully matches annual inflation leaves you underwater for most of the months in between.

None of these are scandals. They are structural features of how pay and prices move at different speeds.

---

## Why averages hide the individual experience

Aggregate wage statistics have a well-known quirk: they measure the average paycheck, not the average person's paycheck change.

When hiring is concentrated at the lower end of the pay scale, the composition of the workforce shifts and average wage growth can look softer than what individual workers actually received. When layoffs hit lower-paid roles, the average can rise even if nobody got a raise. Measures that track the *same* workers over time generally give a truer read on individual pay progress than broad averages do — and they routinely tell a different story.

Two other averaging problems worth knowing:

- **Median vs. mean.** A handful of very large pay packages pulls the average up. The typical worker sits at the median, which usually moves less.
- **Job-switchers vs. job-stayers.** Switching employers has historically produced larger pay bumps than internal raises. Aggregate figures blend both, so the "average raise" overstates what a loyal employee typically receives.

---

## What this does to the wider economy

Consumer spending drives the bulk of U.S. economic activity, so a sustained squeeze on real pay eventually shows up in the data. The usual sequence:

- Households trade down — store brands, cheaper retailers, smaller pack sizes.
- Discretionary categories soften first: dining out, travel upgrades, home goods, subscriptions.
- Savings rates fall and revolving credit balances rise as buffers absorb the gap.
- Companies exposed to lower- and middle-income consumers report weakening volumes even while their revenue holds up on higher prices.

That last pattern — flat or rising revenue on falling unit volumes — is one of the clearest signals that customers are stretched rather than confident.

The offsetting force is the labor market itself. When employers compete for workers, wage growth tends to outrun prices and real pay recovers. When hiring cools, workers lose that leverage and the gap persists longer. Which of those forces dominates is the central question for household finances in 2026.

---

## Practical steps that don't require a raise

You can't set the inflation rate. You can improve your position relative to it.

**Calculate your own number.** Pull twelve months of statements and compare this year's spending to last year's in your five largest categories. That comparison — not the headline rate — is the benchmark your raise has to beat.

**Bring the number into the review.** "Cost of living is up" is easy to deflect. "Here is what I delivered, here is the market rate for this role, and here is the increase needed to hold my compensation steady in real terms" is a business argument. Anchor on market data for your role and region, and ask about the full package — base, bonus, benefit contributions, and flexibility all count.

**Audit the recurring lines first.** Insurance, telecom, subscriptions, and financing costs are where a single hour of work can permanently lower your monthly baseline. Fixed costs compound in your favor when you cut them; variable costs need constant attention to stay cut.

**Watch the categories, not the headline.** If your spending is concentrated in rent, transport, and care, track those specific components rather than the top-line rate. They tell you more about your own trajectory.

**Protect the long-term contributions.** Cutting retirement savings to bridge a short-term gap is expensive in ways that don't show up for decades — particularly when employer matching is involved.

---

## The bottom line

A 3.5% raise is neither good news nor bad news on its own. It is a number waiting for a denominator.

When prices for the things *you* buy rise faster than 3.5%, the raise is a smaller pay cut than no raise would have been — and it's worth saying plainly that this is the reality many households are working through, not a personal failure of budgeting.

Real wages do recover. Historically, they have recovered when price growth cools while the labor market stays firm, and the recovery tends to arrive unevenly, reaching some industries and regions well before others. Knowing which side of that gap you're on — and being able to show it with your own numbers — is the difference between negotiating from a feeling and negotiating from evidence.

---

*This article is general information about economic concepts and is not financial, tax, or investment advice. Figures used are illustrative examples chosen to demonstrate the arithmetic, not reported statistics for any specific period. Economic data is revised regularly; consult official statistical agency releases for current figures and a qualified professional for guidance on your own situation.*

items.title: Hospital Emergency: How Record Heat Waves Are Straining the U.S. Healthcare System
items.body:
Heat has quietly become one of the most demanding public health challenges American hospitals face each summer. Unlike a hurricane or a winter storm, an extended heat wave arrives without wind damage or flooded streets. It does its work slowly, over days, and it shows up in the one place designed to absorb every kind of crisis at once: the emergency department.

Across large parts of the country, the pattern has become familiar. Overnight temperatures stop dropping far enough to let bodies and buildings recover. Air conditioning runs continuously. Utility loads climb. And within about 24 to 72 hours of a heat wave settling in, emergency departments in affected regions begin reporting higher patient volumes, longer waits, and a shift in the type of cases arriving through the door.

This article looks at why heat translates so directly into hospital strain, how health systems are adapting, and what the broader economic and workforce picture looks like.

---

## Why heat lands in the emergency room

Heat-related illness covers a wide range of severity. At the milder end are heat cramps and heat exhaustion — dehydration, dizziness, nausea, heavy sweating. At the severe end is heat stroke, a medical emergency in which the body's ability to regulate its own temperature fails. Public health agencies consistently classify severe heat illness as time-sensitive, which is precisely why it consumes disproportionate emergency department resources: these patients need immediate assessment, cooling, monitoring, and often admission.

But direct heat illness is only part of the story, and in most health systems it is not even the largest part.

The bigger driver is what heat does to existing medical conditions. Sustained high temperatures place additional load on the cardiovascular system, and clinicians widely report increases in cardiac and respiratory presentations during heat events. Kidney function is sensitive to dehydration. Some common medications — including certain diuretics, blood pressure drugs, and psychiatric medications — can affect how the body handles heat or fluid balance. People managing diabetes, COPD, heart failure, or chronic kidney disease are often more vulnerable during a heat wave than during ordinary summer weather.

Then there are the secondary effects. Heat waves are frequently accompanied by degraded air quality, which drives asthma and COPD visits. Power outages during peak demand can leave home oxygen concentrators, refrigerated insulin, and dialysis schedules disrupted. Outdoor workers, athletes, and people without reliable cooling face compounded exposure.

The result is that a single meteorological event produces a broad, mixed surge — not a narrow one that can be handled by adding a single specialty team.

---

## The surge arrives where there is least slack

Emergency departments in the United States were already operating with limited capacity before heat became a recurring seasonal stressor. The core bottleneck is well documented in health policy research: patients who are admitted to the hospital but have no available inpatient bed remain in the emergency department, a situation known as boarding. Every boarded patient occupies a treatment space that a new arrival cannot use.

Heat waves push on this system in several directions at once:

- **Higher arrival volume.** More patients present per hour, often clustered in the late afternoon and evening.
- **Higher acuity mix.** More patients require monitoring, IV fluids, labs, and admission rather than quick treatment and discharge.
- **Longer average stays.** Cooling and rehydration protocols take time; older patients with multiple conditions take longer to stabilize.
- **Slower ambulance turnaround.** When emergency departments are full, EMS crews wait longer to transfer patients, reducing the number of units available in the community.

None of these individually would break a department. Together, sustained over a week, they produce the conditions that hospital administrators describe as capacity strain — a state in which the system still functions but has no margin left for an additional shock.

---

## Who carries the highest risk

Heat risk is not distributed evenly, and understanding the distribution matters for how communities respond.

**Older adults** are consistently identified as the highest-risk group. The physiological ability to sense and dissipate heat declines with age, and older adults are more likely to live alone, take medications that affect thermoregulation, and have limited mobility.

**Infants and young children** have a smaller body mass relative to surface area and depend entirely on caregivers for hydration and environment control.

**Outdoor and non-climate-controlled workers** — in construction, agriculture, warehousing, delivery, and landscaping — face prolonged exposure during the hottest hours. Workplace heat standards vary by state, and this has become an active area of regulatory and legislative debate.

**People with chronic illness or limited housing stability** face the sharpest combination of medical vulnerability and environmental exposure. Access to reliable air conditioning is strongly tied to income, housing age, and neighborhood characteristics. Urban areas with limited tree cover and extensive paved surfaces retain heat overnight — the so-called urban heat island effect — meaning some neighborhoods experience meaningfully hotter nights than others in the same city.

---

## The workforce problem underneath the surge

Healthcare workforce strain in the U.S. is not new, and it is not caused by heat. But heat waves interact badly with an already tight labor picture.

Emergency medicine, critical care, and nursing have all reported elevated burnout since the early 2020s. Surveys conducted across the sector have consistently found that a substantial share of clinical staff report emotional exhaustion, and that intent-to-leave rates rose after the pandemic period. Staffing agencies and travel nursing filled some of the gap at significant cost, and many systems have since worked to reduce that dependence.

Heat events add three specific pressures:

1. **Compressed, unpredictable demand.** Surges concentrated into a few days are harder to staff than steady volume.
2. **Physical strain on staff.** Hospitals themselves are not immune to cooling failures. Older facilities, kitchens, laundry areas, and sterile processing departments can become extremely warm when outdoor temperatures stay high for days.
3. **Cumulative moral fatigue.** Staff who repeatedly manage preventable presentations — patients who lost power, could not afford cooling, or had nowhere to go — report a distinct kind of exhaustion that is separate from workload.

Health systems have responded with a mix of approaches: surge staffing pools, flexible shift structures, on-site rest and hydration protocols, and expanded behavioral health support for employees. The effectiveness of these programs varies widely, and the evidence base is still developing.

---

## The decarbonization paradox

Hospitals are among the most energy-intensive buildings in the commercial sector. They run 24 hours a day, maintain strict temperature and humidity controls, operate imaging and sterilization equipment continuously, and cannot reduce service during peak demand.

At the same time, many health systems have adopted emissions-reduction targets, driven by a combination of institutional commitments, state requirements, procurement standards, and cost management. This creates a genuine tension: heat waves increase cooling demand and backup generator use at exactly the moment a system is trying to lower its energy footprint and its utility costs.

The practical responses being pursued across the sector tend to focus on measures that reduce both emissions and operating cost:

- Building envelope upgrades, reflective roofing, and shading to reduce cooling load
- High-efficiency HVAC and chiller replacement, often the single largest energy line item
- On-site solar generation and battery storage, which can also improve resilience during grid stress
- Combined heat and power systems and microgrids for critical care areas
- Waste anesthetic gas capture, which addresses a small but potent emissions source
- Supply chain and procurement changes, which account for a large share of total healthcare emissions

None of these is a quick fix. Capital projects in hospital settings take years and must be sequenced around clinical operations. But the direction is consistent: resilience and efficiency investments increasingly get evaluated together rather than separately.

---

## What effective preparation looks like

The cities and health systems that manage heat waves best tend to share a few characteristics.

**Early, tiered activation.** Heat action plans that trigger on forecast rather than on observed emergency department volume give responders a head start. Many regions now use thresholds that account for overnight lows and humidity, not just daytime highs.

**Cooling access.** Public cooling centers, extended library and community center hours, and transportation to reach them address the population that has no cooling at home.

**Proactive outreach.** Wellness checks for isolated older adults, coordinated through utilities, home health agencies, and community organizations, are among the more effective interventions.

**Utility protections.** Seasonal moratoriums on disconnections and priority restoration for medically dependent customers reduce a specific, preventable pathway into the emergency department.

**Workplace standards.** Mandatory rest breaks, shade, water access, and acclimatization schedules for new workers are established occupational safety practices in high-heat industries.

**Clear public communication.** Practical, plainly worded guidance tends to outperform severity messaging alone.

---

## Practical guidance during a heat wave

General public health guidance during extreme heat is consistent and straightforward:

- Stay in air-conditioned spaces during the hottest hours where possible; fans alone provide limited protection at very high temperatures.
- Drink water regularly rather than waiting for thirst, unless a clinician has advised fluid restriction.
- Limit strenuous outdoor activity to early morning or evening.
- Check on older neighbors, relatives living alone, and anyone with a chronic condition.
- Never leave children or pets in a parked vehicle, where interior temperatures rise rapidly.
- Learn the warning signs of heat exhaustion — heavy sweating, weakness, nausea, headache, dizziness — and treat them seriously.
- Seek emergency care immediately for confusion, fainting, seizure, hot dry skin, or a very high body temperature. These are signs of a medical emergency.

If you take prescription medication or manage a chronic condition, it is worth asking your own clinician before summer whether your treatment plan needs any seasonal adjustment.

---

## The outlook

The structural picture is unlikely to change quickly. Summers with extended high-heat stretches are now a planning assumption for most U.S. health systems rather than an exception, and the emergency department remains the default point of contact for anyone who cannot get care elsewhere.

What is changing is the framing. Heat is increasingly treated as an operational and infrastructure problem rather than a purely clinical one — a question of housing quality, grid reliability, tree canopy, workplace rules, and building systems as much as of triage protocols. Health systems that have made progress generally did so by working upstream, in partnership with municipal agencies and utilities, well before the first advisory of the season.

That is a slower, less visible kind of emergency response. It is also, by most accounts, the one that reduces the number of people who end up in an emergency department in the first place.

---

*This article is intended as general information about public health and healthcare system operations. It is not medical advice and should not be used to diagnose or treat any condition. If you have a health concern, consult a qualified healthcare professional. In a medical emergency in the United States, call 911.*

items.title: The Hollowed-Out Downtown: How Remote Work Rewrote the Math of America's Office Market
items.body:
For most of the postwar era, the American downtown ran on a simple assumption: companies would keep needing more desks, and those desks would keep being downtown. Cities built their tax bases, transit systems, and street-level economies on that assumption. Investors underwrote billions of dollars in office towers on it.

That assumption broke in 2020, and — unlike the temporary shocks of previous recessions — it never fully repaired itself. Six years later, the working-from-home share of paid days in the United States has settled at roughly a quarter to a third, several times the pre-pandemic rate of around 7 percent, according to long-running surveys from the WFH Research project run by economists at Stanford, the University of Chicago, and ITAM. Return-to-office mandates pulled attendance up from the 2021 trough, but they did not restore the five-day office week. Hybrid, not remote, became the equilibrium — and hybrid still means a company that once leased 100,000 square feet now needs perhaps 60,000 to 80,000.

Multiplied across a national office stock measured in billions of square feet, that arithmetic produces one of the largest repricings of a single asset class in modern American history.

## What the "trillion-dollar" number actually measures

Headline estimates of office value destruction range widely, and it is worth understanding why before treating any single figure as fact.

A widely cited working paper by economists Arpit Gupta, Vrinda Mittal, and Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh, published through the National Bureau of Economic Research, modeled remote work's effect on office cash flows and lease renewals and projected long-run value declines in the hundreds of billions of dollars for U.S. office alone. Separately, the McKinsey Global Institute estimated that office values across nine major global cities could fall by roughly $800 billion by 2030 in a moderate scenario, and by well over $1 trillion in a more severe one.

Figures approaching $2 trillion generally come from broader framings — global rather than U.S.-only, or including the knock-on effects on retail, hotels, and municipal revenue rather than office buildings in isolation. None of these are audited losses. They are model outputs, sensitive to assumptions about interest rates, lease expiration schedules, and how much space tenants ultimately give back.

What is not modeled is the observable part: buildings that have traded hands at 50 to 80 percent below their previous sale price. Over the past three years, offices in Manhattan, Chicago's Loop, downtown Los Angeles, San Francisco, Washington, and St. Louis have all sold at steep discounts to prices paid in the 2014–2019 cycle. Several changed hands for less than the cost of the land beneath them. Those transactions are not projections — they are comparables, and appraisers use them to reprice everything nearby.

## Why vacancy turned into devaluation so slowly, then so fast

Office leases are long. A tenant that decided in 2021 to cut its footprint in half may not have been able to act on that decision until a 2026 expiration. This is the central reason the office correction has unfolded as a slow bleed rather than a crash: the damage arrives one lease expiration at a time.

Three forces then compounded it.

**Vacancy climbed to records.** National office vacancy has hovered around 20 percent, the highest level in the more than four decades Moody's Analytics has tracked the series. Availability — which includes space that is leased but being marketed for sublease — runs several points higher still.

**Financing costs reset.** A building generating the same rent is worth materially less when the discount rate rises. The interest rate cycle that began in 2022 devalued all real estate; office simply had no rent growth to offset it.

**The debt came due.** The Mortgage Bankers Association has estimated that close to $1 trillion of commercial mortgages were scheduled to mature in 2025, with heavy volumes following. Loans written when a tower was 92 percent leased and rates were near zero cannot always be refinanced when it is 65 percent leased and rates are not. Office delinquency rates in commercial mortgage-backed securities climbed into the double digits — exceeding the peaks recorded after the 2008 financial crisis, according to data firm Trepp — and lenders have increasingly chosen extensions, discounted payoffs, or deed-in-lieu handovers rather than forcing sales into a thin market.

## Not one market, but two

The most consistent misreading of this story treats "office" as a single asset. It is not.

Newer, amenity-rich, well-located buildings — the trophy tier — have held occupancy and in several markets have posted record asking rents. Companies shrinking their footprints have frequently upgraded them at the same time, using better space as an argument for coming in. Developers built comparatively little new office during the 2020s, so the supply of genuinely top-tier space is limited.

The pain concentrates in the tier below: 1970s and 1980s commodity towers with deep floor plates, dated systems, single-pane curtain walls, and no realistic capital budget for renovation. Many of these buildings are not temporarily underleased. They are functionally obsolete, and their highest-value use may no longer be as offices at all.

This bifurcation matters for policy, because a citywide vacancy average conceals it. A downtown can post 22 percent vacancy while its best five buildings are full and its worst twenty are effectively empty.

## The municipal squeeze

For city governments, the transmission channel is property tax.

Commercial property is assessed on income. When income falls, assessments follow — sometimes after a lag, often after litigation. In cities where downtown commercial parcels carry an outsized share of the levy, a reassessment cycle can open a structural hole in the operating budget. Boston, which draws roughly 70 percent of its revenue from property taxes and historically taxes commercial property at a higher rate than residential, has drawn particular attention from analysts at the Tufts Center for State Policy Analysis and elsewhere for that concentration. San Francisco, New York, Chicago, and Washington face variations on the same problem.

The knock-on effects are less visible than the budget line but just as real. Downtown lunch counters, dry cleaners, parking operators, and transit agencies were all sized for a five-day commuter population. Transit systems that once covered a large share of operating costs from fares have seen ridership recover unevenly, with weekday peaks flattened even where weekend travel has fully returned.

The pessimistic framing of this is the "urban doom loop": falling values cut revenue, revenue cuts degrade services, degraded services push out residents and employers, and values fall further. It is a coherent risk, and it deserves to be taken seriously. But it is a scenario, not a forecast. Cities are not passive in it, and the evidence of the past two years is that many are acting.

## Conversion: real, growing, and not a cure-all

The obvious answer to empty offices in a country short of housing is to turn one into the other. The obvious answer is also harder than it sounds.

Postwar office towers were designed around large floor plates with deep interior cores — space that is fine for cubicles and impossible for bedrooms, which need windows. Plumbing risers built for a few restrooms per floor must be multiplied for dozens of kitchens and bathrooms. Facades often cannot be opened. Zoning may forbid residential use outright. And the arithmetic only works when the acquisition price is low enough to absorb $200 to $500 per square foot of retrofit cost, which in practice means the seller must accept a deeply discounted price first.

Even so, the pipeline has grown substantially. CBRE and other brokerages have tracked well over 70 million square feet of U.S. office slated for conversion, with completions hitting successive records over the past two years — still only a low single-digit percentage of national inventory, but heavily concentrated in exactly the downtowns that need it.

Policy has moved to close the gap:

- **New York City** created an Office Conversion Accelerator to shepherd projects through permitting, paired it with a state tax exemption for conversions that include affordable units, and passed the City of Yes for Housing Opportunity zoning amendments in late 2024 to widen eligibility.
- **Washington, D.C.** has offered a multiyear tax abatement for downtown residential conversions as part of an explicit downtown population target.
- **Boston** launched a conversion program offering long-term partial property tax abatements to make retrofit math work.
- **Chicago** anchored its LaSalle Street Reimagined initiative on public subsidy tied to affordable housing requirements.
- **Calgary**, outside the U.S. but the most-studied case in North America, committed substantial public funding to a per-square-foot conversion grant and has removed several million square feet of office from its downtown inventory.

A quieter parallel track is demolition. Removing a functionally obsolete building from the inventory improves the market for everything left standing, and in some cases a surface lot with development optionality is worth more than a tower with negative cash flow.

## What to watch next

The office correction is now mature enough that the useful questions have shifted from "how bad" to "how does it resolve."

**Does leasing volume keep recovering?** Leasing activity in major markets has improved from the trough, and several central business districts have posted positive net absorption after years of negative readings. Sustained absorption, more than any price index, is the signal that demand has found its floor.

**How much space gets permanently removed?** Conversion plus demolition is the only mechanism that fixes oversupply structurally. Watch inventory, not just vacancy.

**Do the loans clear?** Extensions bought time; they did not resolve losses. The pace at which distressed office debt is actually written down and recapitalized determines whether the sector's overhang lifts in three years or ten.

**Do downtowns become residential?** The most durable version of the recovery is not offices refilling — it is central business districts becoming central neighborhoods, with a resident population that supports street-level commerce seven days a week rather than five.

That transition is expensive, slow, and unevenly feasible across cities. It is also, in most of the serious proposals now on the table, the actual plan. The trillion-dollar figure describes what was lost on one side of the ledger. What gets built on the other side is still being decided.

---

*This article is general information about commercial real estate and municipal finance trends. Figures cited are estimates from the named research organizations and industry data providers; methodologies and totals vary meaningfully between sources and are revised over time. Nothing here is investment, tax, or legal advice.*

items.title: Open Weights Go Mainstream: How GitHub's Coding Model Rewrites Enterprise AI Strategy
items.body:
For most of the past three years, the enterprise AI conversation had a comfortable shape. You picked a frontier lab, signed an enterprise agreement, wired your developers into a proprietary endpoint, and treated the model itself as a fixed input — expensive, capable, and somebody else's problem.

GitHub's decision to publish an open-weight coding model breaks that shape. Not because open models are new — they aren't — but because of who is doing the publishing. When the platform that hosts the world's source code and sits inside millions of developer workflows says the weights are yours to download, the model stops being a scarce resource and starts being a component.

That distinction is the whole story. Components get commoditized. Scarce resources get monetized.

## What "open-weight" actually means — and what it doesn't

The terminology matters here, because a lot of coverage flattens it.

**Open-weight** means the trained parameters are downloadable. You can run the model on your own hardware, inspect its behavior, fine-tune it on your own data, and — depending on the license — ship it inside a product.

**Open-source**, in the traditional software sense, would additionally mean access to training data, training code, and an OSI-approved license with no use restrictions. Very few widely-used models clear that bar.

The gap between those two is where most enterprise legal reviews get stuck. An open-weight release can still carry acceptable-use clauses, redistribution conditions, revenue thresholds that trigger different terms, or restrictions on using outputs to train competing models. None of that makes a model unusable. It does mean that "it's open" is the beginning of a procurement conversation, not the end of one.

Practical translation for anyone building a strategy on this: read the actual license text before the architecture diagram gets drawn. The difference between a permissive license and a conditional one can decide whether your product roadmap is viable.

## Why a developer platform releasing weights hits differently

Independent labs have released strong open models for a while. What changes when the release comes from inside the developer toolchain is *distribution physics*.

A model published by a research lab has to earn its way into a workflow. A model published by the company that already owns the repository, the pull request, the CI pipeline, and the code review surface arrives pre-integrated into the place where the work happens. Adoption friction collapses.

That has three downstream effects worth taking seriously:

1. **The floor rises for everyone.** Capability that was a paid differentiator eighteen months ago becomes a baseline you can self-host. Vendors selling *only* that capability lose their pricing power.
2. **Evaluation becomes the bottleneck.** When switching models is a config change rather than a contract renegotiation, the constraint moves from "can we get access?" to "can we tell which one is actually better for our codebase?"
3. **The build-versus-buy line moves — in both directions.** Some things get cheaper to build in-house. Others (reliability, security review, ops) get more clearly worth buying.

## The commoditization thesis, honestly stated

The strong version of the argument goes: models are converging, open weights track closed weights with a shrinking lag, inference cost falls on a steep curve, and therefore the model layer collapses into undifferentiated infrastructure — the way databases, web servers, and operating system kernels did before it.

There is real evidence for this. Capability gaps between the best closed model and the best open model at a given task have narrowed repeatedly. Serving costs per token have fallen sharply across the industry. Quantization and distillation keep pushing decent performance onto smaller and cheaper hardware.

But the thesis has genuine limits, and enterprises that ignore them get burned:

- **The frontier is not commoditized.** Open weights tend to trail the frontier, and the hardest tasks — long-horizon agentic work, complex multi-step reasoning, novel domains — are exactly where the gap persists longest.
- **"Free weights" is not "free model."** Self-hosting moves cost from a line item to a headcount. GPU capacity, serving infrastructure, latency engineering, uptime, security patching, and evaluation all become yours. For many workloads, a managed API is genuinely cheaper on total cost of ownership.
- **Commoditization is uneven.** Autocomplete-grade code generation commoditizes fast. Reliable autonomous refactoring across a large legacy monorepo does not.

The useful mental model isn't "open replaces closed." It's tiering: cheap, self-hosted, private models handle the high-volume, well-defined majority of work, while frontier APIs handle the hard tail — and the ratio shifts over time.

## Where the value actually migrates

If the model is the commodity, what isn't?

**Proprietary data and context.** A general model that has read all public code still hasn't read your internal service conventions, your deprecated-API graveyard, or the three years of incident postmortems that explain why a module is written the way it is. Retrieval quality, context assembly, and internal knowledge plumbing are compounding advantages that no model release erases.

**Evaluation infrastructure.** The company that can answer "does this model actually reduce our defect rate?" with data will make better decisions than the company arguing about benchmark charts. Benchmarks measure general capability; they don't measure your codebase. Task-specific evals built on your own repositories and your own definition of "correct" are the durable asset.

**Workflow integration and trust.** The gap between a model producing correct code and an organization *safely shipping* that code is filled with review policy, test coverage, permissions design, audit trails, and rollback discipline. That's organizational engineering, not model selection.

**Governance and data residency.** For regulated sectors, the ability to run a capable model entirely inside a controlled boundary — no third-party inference, no data egress — is not a cost optimization. It's the difference between a project existing and not existing. This is arguably the single largest concrete enterprise benefit of open weights.

## A practical playbook

For teams reassessing strategy right now, five moves are defensible regardless of how the market shakes out.

**1. Build a portability layer, and mean it.** Route every model call through an internal abstraction — your own service, a gateway, or a well-maintained adapter. If swapping a provider requires touching application code in fifty places, you've locked yourself in by architecture rather than by contract. This is cheap to do early and painful to retrofit.

**2. Build the eval harness before you need it.** Assemble a private test set from your own code: real tasks, real acceptance criteria, real failure modes. Run every candidate model against it. This turns model selection from a debate into a measurement, and it's the asset that keeps paying off with every subsequent release.

**3. Tier your workloads deliberately.** Classify tasks by difficulty, latency tolerance, and data sensitivity. Push the high-volume, low-complexity, high-sensitivity work toward self-hosted open weights. Keep the hard tail on the strongest available model. Revisit the split quarterly, because the boundary moves.

**4. Do the total-cost math with real numbers.** Compare API pricing against fully loaded self-hosting cost: hardware or reserved capacity, utilization rate, engineering time, on-call burden, and the evaluation work you'd have to do anyway. Self-hosting wins decisively at high, steady volume. It loses badly at low or spiky volume. Know which one you are.

**5. Get legal in early, once.** One thorough license and acceptable-use review, documented and reusable, beats a scramble at launch. Cover redistribution, fine-tuned derivatives, output ownership, and any downstream customer-facing use.

## What to watch next

Three signals will tell you which way this is actually going.

Watch whether **capability parity holds at the agentic tier** — not on single-function benchmarks, but on long, multi-file, multi-step work where errors compound. That's where a real gap still lives.

Watch **licensing drift**. If major open-weight releases keep loosening terms, commercial adoption accelerates. If they tighten as competition intensifies, the practical openness of "open" narrows.

Watch **pricing response from proprietary vendors**. Sustained price cuts, more generous free tiers, or a pivot toward selling agents, tooling, and integration rather than raw tokens would all confirm that the model layer is compressing and value is moving up the stack.

## The bottom line

The strategic error is treating this as a binary — open or closed, self-host or API. It isn't. It's a portfolio decision that needs to be re-run as costs and capabilities move, and the organizations that do well will be the ones that made switching cheap before they needed to switch.

The model was never the moat. It was just the part that was easiest to point at. What GitHub's release makes harder to ignore is that the defensible work — your data, your evaluations, your workflow, your governance — is the work that was always going to matter, and it's the work no one can download.

---

*Analysis and commentary. Details of any specific model release — including licensing terms, capabilities, and availability — should be verified against the official announcement and license text before being relied upon for procurement or engineering decisions. This article is general information, not legal, financial, or investment advice.*
